prompt: According to Steve Yegge's account of Jeff Bezos's internal API mandate at Amazon (recounted in "Stevey's Google Platforms Rant"), what was the core requirement placed on every team?
choices: Every team must migrate to Java within one year
Teams must expose their data and functionality only through service interfaces, with no direct back-door access to another team's data store
Every internal service must be released as an open-source project
Teams must buy rather than build all of their infrastructure

prompt: A small startup needs enterprise SSO/SAML working within six weeks to close a deal, and SSO is not something that differentiates their product from competitors. Using the build-vs-buy criteria from the lesson, which choice is best supported?
choices: Buy a narrow SSO/SCIM product (like WorkOS or Clerk) because it optimizes for time-to-market and inherited compliance on a capability that isn't a differentiator
Roll their own SAML implementation from scratch, since owning the code always minimizes long-term risk
Self-host Keycloak, since it's free and therefore always the lowest-cost option
Postpone the deal until a full internal identity platform can be built in-house

prompt: Why did GitHub build its own custom code-search engine (Blackbird), described in their March 2023 engineering blog, instead of continuing to scale Elasticsearch for github.com code search?
choices: Elastic discontinued the open-source license GitHub depended on
GitHub's exact-match and regex search requirements at their scale had outgrown what a general-purpose search product could serve efficiently
A data-residency law required GitHub to remove all third-party search vendors
Elasticsearch could not be run inside a Kubernetes cluster

prompt: Spotify's Backstage (open-sourced 2020, now a CNCF project) is used in the lesson as a good developer-experience example because of its 'golden path' templates. What specifically makes this good DX, contrasted with a ticket-gated infrastructure request?
choices: It lets engineers self-service scaffold a new service — with CI, deploy pipeline, and catalog entry wired up — in minutes, instead of waiting days on a manually reviewed ticket
It requires every engineer to use the exact same programming language for all services
It replaces the need for any platform team to exist
It is primarily a chat tool for filing infrastructure tickets faster

prompt: What is the central argument of the SPACE framework (Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Houck, and Butler, ACM Queue 2021) about measuring developer productivity?
choices: A single metric, such as commit count or lines of code, is sufficient to measure productivity
Productivity should be measured across five dimensions — Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication, and Efficiency — rather than collapsed into one number
Only deployment frequency matters, since it is the sole DORA metric worth tracking
Developer productivity cannot be meaningfully measured under any circumstances

prompt: Segment's 2020 post "Goodbye Microservices" described consolidating roughly 140 small services back into one monolith. Per the lesson, what was the primary documented driver behind that decision?
choices: Cloud compute costs for running many small services became unaffordable
The operational and cognitive overhead of debugging and on-call across hundreds of independently deployed services outweighed the isolation benefits for that workload
A company-wide executive mandate banned microservices outright
Kubernetes reached end-of-life and forced a redesign

prompt: Using Wardley Mapping's evolution axis (genesis, custom-built, product, commodity/utility), where should a company's actual product differentiator sit relative to a commodity capability like standard SSO/auth, and what does that imply for where build effort should go?
choices: Both should be treated identically, since evolution stage doesn't affect sourcing decisions

The differentiator typically sits closer to genesis/custom-built, while SSO/auth sits at product/commodity — so build effort belongs on the differentiator, and commodity capabilities should generally be bought
Commodity capabilities should always be built in-house to maximize long-term control
Genesis-stage capabilities should always be purchased from the most mature vendor available

prompt: A staff engineer is writing a technical strategy document to align four teams on adopting a shared event schema registry. Per the lesson's guidance (modeled on Segment's strategy-doc structure), which element is most essential to keep the doc from becoming an ignored wiki page?
choices: An exhaustive enumeration of every conceivable future edge case the registry might encounter
A concrete decision with an owner, a migration plan with dates, and a stated condition for when the decision should be revisited
A requirement that all four teams rewrite their entire codebases within a single sprint
Omitting any discussion of trade-offs or rejected alternatives so the decision cannot be challenged
